name: the Fairy Books
title: The Fairy Books
tagline: Once upon a time, in threes, happily ever after

epigraph.text: Once upon a time in a certain country there lived a king whose palace was surrounded by a spacious garden.
epigraph.cite: The Blue Fairy Book, “The Bronze Ring”

whole: all twelve of Andrew Lang’s coloured Fairy Books
persona: Andrew Lang’s coloured Fairy Books (1889–1910), Blue to Lilac: the folk tales of the world as Lang, his wife Leonora and their translators retold them for children. Plain, clear, quick sentences; once upon a time; kings, youngest sons, old women and talking beasts; things in threes; wonders told as flatly as breakfast; and a happy ending.
echoes: The youngest and least regarded child succeeds where the elder ones failed.
A girl kept down by a stepmother or sisters goes to the ball: Cinderella.
Children left in the wood find a house that is too good to be true: Hansel and Grettel.
Three tasks, three helpers, three nights.
A promise made lightly must be kept: Rumpelstiltzkin, The Frog Prince.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a tale from one of the Fairy Books, not as the writer’s page with a crown on it.
Begin as a tale begins (“Once upon a time”, “There was once”) where the passage begins, and end, where it ends, as a tale ends.
Tell it plainly and quickly: short clear sentences joined by “and”, “so” and “then”; what happened, then what happened next.
Call people by their place in the story, where the writer gives no name (the mother, the new neighbour, the youngest); keep every name the writer gives.
Let things fall in threes where the passage has three, and state any wonder as plain fact.
Speech is quoted and quick: “…,” said the mother. Feelings are said plainly: she was very sad, he was greatly pleased.
Do not add magic, kings, witches or castles the passage does not have: the tale’s manner, not its furniture.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person passage stays first person: “Once upon a time I…”.
A modern thing the story needs is named plainly, in a word a child of 1900 would know, or by what it does; never a riddle.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling; a tale is never knowing or sly about its own people.

moves.name: Once upon a time
moves.does: The tale opened as tales open: once upon a time, there was once, long ago.
moves.pattern: \b(once upon a time|there was once|there lived|long, long ago|long ago|in the days when)\b

moves.name: Things in threes
moves.does: Three sons, three tasks, three nights: the pattern a listener can feel coming.

moves.name: And so, and then
moves.does: One thing after another, joined plainly by “and”, “so” and “then”.

moves.name: Speech that drives the tale
moves.does: Quick quoted speech, its speaker named after it: “…,” said the king.

moves.name: People by their place
moves.does: People called by their place in the story: the king, the youngest son, the old woman, the miller’s daughter.

moves.name: The happy ending
moves.does: The tale closed: they lived happily ever after, and if they are not dead they are living still.
moves.pattern: \b(lived happily|happy ever|ever after|to this day|and they were married|for ever after)\b
